text: Synthetic data is artificially generated, often by another model, to stand in for real data. Organizations reach for it for reasonable reasons, but it doesn't automatically escape any of the concerns covered earlier in this chapter.

It fills gaps where real examples of a rare but important case are scarce, augments a small dataset with more examples to learn from, and sometimes avoids containing any single real person's actual information. Those are legitimate reasons. But none of the earlier concerns disappear just because the data wasn't directly collected.

It still encodes the patterns of whatever real data it was modeled on, if that underlying data had a bias, the synthetic data can reproduce and even amplify it, with no single real example you can point to. It doesn't automatically protect privacy, a synthetic record generated by closely mimicking real records can still leak identifiable details, synthetic is not a synonym for anonymous, that has to be verified. And quality still applies, the same dimensions from two lessons ago don't go away because the data was generated rather than collected.

The one genuinely new question is documentation honesty. A model trained partly on synthetic data needs that fact recorded clearly, not blended invisibly into the training data as if it were all collected the same way. Anyone evaluating the model's behavior needs to know which parts were real-world observation and which were generated, because the two carry different risks.

Synthetic data is a legitimate tool, not a shortcut around governance, it still needs provenance, a bias check, and the same quality bar, plus one disclosure real data doesn't require. That closes Chapter Two. Next up: Chapter Three, model documentation and model cards.
